The 4P Agent

Hi, I'm Ken Huang, CEO of DistributedApps.ai. In this video I walk through my deck on the 4P agent: agents that start conversations, keep running, and hold both personal and company data. I explain what the term means, compare seven products that fit it, and cover four security risks that I think need a threat model of their own.
About Ken Huang

A quick word about me. I lead the OWASP AIVSS project, I co-chair AI safety working groups at the Cloud Security Alliance, and I teach as an adjunct professor at the University of San Francisco. I have also written books on AI security and agentic AI with Springer, Cambridge, Wiley and Packt. My threat modeling work is the background for this talk.
Seven Launches, One Design

Between May and October 2026, seven companies published launch material for the same agent design. Yet the security teams I work with still design controls for an agent that waits for a prompt, finishes one task, and forgets what it did. The launch posts describe something different: an agent that starts the conversation, keeps working after the user leaves, and remembers. So the question a threat model must now answer is this: what does an agent with standing access do while no person is monitoring it?
The Four Ps

Based on my research, I coined the term 4P agent for agents that combine four properties: proactive, persistent, personal and professional. Engineers have shipped each property alone for years. What is new in 2026 is that product teams put all four into one agent and gave that agent a computer of its own in the cloud. Each property increases the effect of the others. In my view, that amplification, not any single feature, defines the category.
Proactive and Persistent

Each property has a test a buyer can apply. Proactive: who sends the first message of the working day? The product passes when the agent does. Persistent, in the running sense: does the agent stay on after the user closes the laptop or locks the phone? Persistent, in the remembering sense: does the agent use what it stored in later weeks? In practice, a scheduled job and chat memory become one process, and the agent keeps preferences, open commitments and the names of important people.
Personal and Professional

Personal means two people can give the same instruction and get different results, because the agent knows different things about each of them. Professional means the agent finishes a work process, such as preparing a meeting or chasing an unpaid invoice, through the systems employees use. So the same agent holds a household's mail and calendars and a company's mail tenant, CRM and ledger. Depending on how the maker built it, the agent runs inside the company's identity, data loss prevention and audit controls, or outside them.
Seven 4P Agents Compared

Here are seven 4P agents compared: Claude Duet, Meta Muse, OpenAI Dots, Instinct, Gemini Spark, Microsoft Autopilot and Poke. Full means the source describes the property with no stated limit, Partial means a stated limit, and Limited means the material does not describe it. All seven score Full on proactive. OpenAI Dots is the only one scored Full on all four. The makers differ most in approval design, and in whether the agent runs in a consumer account or inside a company tenant.
Four Risks, Three Frameworks

The 4P design adds four risks that a chat assistant waiting for prompts did not have: standing access, memory poisoning, agent-started actions and delegated authority. Early Instinct users reported incidents matching three of them within weeks of launch. I classify each risk against three frameworks I work on: OWASP AIVSS, which scores agentic vulnerabilities; the OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10; and MAESTRO, the seven-layer threat model I introduced through the Cloud Security Alliance. Of the four, agent-started actions have the largest agentic amplification.
Risk 1: Standing Access

Risk one is standing access. An agent that checks an inbox on its own schedule cannot wait for the user to sign in, so mail, chat, files and often payment methods stay connected all the time. An attacker who compromises a chat assistant gets one conversation. An attacker who compromises a 4P agent gets every connected account at once, during hours when nobody is watching. Forbes reports that Instinct kept Claire Vo's emails after she disconnected Gmail. The control I rate highest today is credential separation: the model uses a login it never reads.
Risk 2: Memory Poisoning

Risk two is memory poisoning. Every day, a 4P agent reads mail from strangers and writes notes from it into long-term memory. That can turn a one-time prompt injection into an instruction the agent keeps following weeks later. Vellum reports that Alex Cohen emailed his own inbox a set of malicious instructions, and that Instinct followed them. My proposed fix is to record the source of every stored memory entry, so what the user stated is kept apart from what an outside sender wrote.
Risk 3: Agent-Started Actions

Risk three is agent-started actions. In a chat product, every action starts from a prompt the user typed. With a 4P agent, the user often learns about an action from the agent's own report. Forbes reports that one Instinct user watched the agent book a table with a large cancellation fee. Makers put the check in three places. OpenAI restricts the agent to read-only tools while the user is away. Meta adds a second agent, called Sentinel, that must approve anything sent to the internet. Anthropic, Google and Microsoft require approval for named classes of action. I think approval per class of action, such as payments, sends, deletes and signatures, works better than approval per tool.
Risk 4: Delegated Authority

Risk four is delegated authority. Every action runs under some identity, and that identity decides who can audit the action and who is accountable for a mistake. Makers split into two models. In one, the agent has its own identity, as with Microsoft Autopilot and its governed Entra identity, so auditors can attribute each action. In the other, the agent acts as the user under terms of service, as Vellum reports for Instinct, and the user carries the consequences. When one agent holds a family calendar and a company CRM, personal data can appear in a work message, and the company's data loss controls see it only when the agent runs inside the company tenant.
Builder's Verdict

My verdict as a builder: the makers now compete on control design more than on capability. The largest AI labs and two startups now sell one agent design. Every incident in this deck comes from Instinct, the one product with no documented approval rules, according to Vellum. The makers list three next steps: more agents per user, more access to the user's own devices, and stronger isolation from the maker, such as Meta's Confidential VM with keys held only by the user.
